01.note: A man everyone took to be Jewish came to Rabbi Yehuda and said he had converted in private, so he was not really Jewish. Rabbi Yehuda asked whether he had witnesses; he had none. He asked whether he had children; he did. Rabbi Yehuda told him he was believed about himself, and so could disqualify himself from marrying a Jewish woman, but he was not believed when it came to disqualifying his children.
01.why: Rabbi Yehuda has just ruled that a conversion done in private, without a court, is not valid. The Gemara then asks how his ruling here fits his other teaching that a father is believed about his children's status, and offers two explanations.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who held that a conversion done privately, outside a court, is not valid; the man brings his claim to him.

terms.meaning: A non-Jew who formally joins the Jewish people. Rabbi Yehuda held this had to be done before a court to count.

02.note: Three Sages, Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha, were sitting in Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha's courtyard and talking. They recalled a city in the Land of Israel whose slaves refused to be circumcised. The masters put up with them for twelve months and then sold them to gentiles. The Sages asked whose opinion the townspeople had followed; the story itself does not give the answer.
02.why: The discussion is about when a Jewish master may keep an uncircumcised slave. The Gemara answers the Sages' question with a teaching that a master may wait up to twelve months before selling such a slave to gentiles.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappi
people.about: One of the three Sages talking in the courtyard.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: One of the three Sages talking in the courtyard.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa
people.about: One of the three Sages; the conversation takes place in his courtyard.

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel.
Non-Jews.

03.note: Rav Dimi brought a report from the Land of Israel: a girl in the village of Hitlu was sweeping the house when a village dog sodomized her from behind. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled she was still permitted to marry a priest. Shmuel added that she was permitted even to a High Priest. The Gemara objects that there was no High Priest in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's day, and explains that Shmuel meant she would be fit for one.
03.why: Rabbi Shimi bar Hiyya has just ruled that a woman who had intercourse with an animal is not considered a harlot and may marry a priest; this case is the precedent. The Gemara then asks for the verse showing there is no harlotry with an animal.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who brought this report when he came from the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who ruled the girl could still marry a priest.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who added that she was fit even for a High Priest.

terms.meaning: Here, marriage to a priest (kohen). Priests may not marry a woman considered a harlot, and a High Priest must marry a virgin.
The chief priest who served in the Temple; there was none after the Temple was destroyed.

04.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi told of a city in the Land of Israel where a family's lineage was challenged. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sent Rabbi Romanus to investigate. He found that the family included a woman who had converted before she was three years and a day old and had married a priest, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled she was permitted to the priesthood. When Rabbi Zeira asked whether he had drawn his ruling from this case, Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi said he had heard it from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explicitly.
04.why: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi had reported that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules like Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai, who permits a girl converted before age three to marry a priest. Rabbi Zeira wanted to know whether this was said outright or only inferred from this case.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: The Sage who reported the case.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who sent an investigator and permitted the woman to the priesthood.

people.name: Rabbi Romanus
people.about: The Sage sent to examine the family's lineage.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi
people.about: Transmitted Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling and insists he heard it directly.

terms.meaning: The age below which, in Talmudic law, intercourse does not count as removing a girl's virginity. A girl converted before then could be treated as never having had relations as a gentile.

05.note: A priest married a woman who had converted before she was three years and a day old. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak challenged him. The priest answered that Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi had reported, in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's name, that the law follows Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai, who permits such a marriage. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak told him to divorce her, and said that otherwise he would remove Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi from his ear.
05.why: The Gemara has just shown that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules like Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai on such a convert marrying a priest. This case shows a Sage refusing to rely on that ruling in practice.

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
people.about: The Sage who ordered the priest to divorce his wife.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi
people.about: The Sage whose report the priest relied on.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: The Sage in whose name the ruling was reported.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai
people.about: The Sage whose opinion the priest claimed to follow.

terms.meaning: A kohen, a descendant of Aaron. Priests are barred from certain marriages, including, in the view of most Sages, to a woman who converted.
Jewish law; the binding ruling.

06.note: Yehoshua ben Gamla, a priest, betrothed Marta bat Baitos, a widow. The king then appointed him High Priest, and he went ahead and married her. Rav Yosef saw a conspiracy in the wording that the king appointed him, and cited Rav Asi: Marta bat Baitos brought King Yannai a vessel full of dinars until he made Yehoshua ben Gamla High Priest.
06.why: The mishna rules that a priest who betrothed a widow and was then appointed High Priest may still marry her, and cites this marriage as the example. The Gemara then reads the wording closely and finds that the appointment was bought.

people.name: Yehoshua ben Gamla
people.about: A priest who betrothed a widow and was then made High Priest.

people.name: Marta bat Baitos
people.about: The widow he betrothed; Rav Asi says she paid the king to appoint him.

people.name: King Yannai
people.about: The king who made Yehoshua ben Gamla High Priest.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who saw a conspiracy behind the appointment.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: The Sage who reported the payment to the king.

terms.meaning: The first stage of Jewish marriage, which already makes the couple legally bound; the wedding itself comes later.
The chief priest of the Temple. The Torah forbids him to marry a widow.
The brother of a man who died childless; he is obligated to marry the widow (levirate marriage) or release her.
A measure of volume, half a se'a, used here for the size of a vessel full of coins.

07.note: Rabbi Akiva taught that one who had students in his youth should have more in his old age. The Gemara illustrates: he had twelve thousand pairs of students from Gevat to Antipatris, and all of them died in one period because they did not treat each other with respect. The world was desolate of Torah until he went to the Sages in the South and taught five new students, Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua, who upheld the Torah. It is taught that the first students all died between Passover and Shavuot, a bad death, which Rav Nahman says was diphtheria.
07.why: The Gemara is discussing whether a man who already has children should have more. Rabbi Yehoshua reads a verse from Ecclesiastes to say yes, and Rabbi Akiva reads the same verse about students, which his own life illustrates.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A great teacher whose first twelve thousand pairs of students died; he then taught five new ones.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: One of Rabbi Akiva's later students who upheld the Torah.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: One of Rabbi Akiva's later students.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: One of Rabbi Akiva's later students.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Identifies the bad death the students died as diphtheria.

terms.meaning: The festival seven weeks after Passover.
A throat infection that can choke a person to death.

08.note: Rabbi Elazar taught that all craftsmen will one day work the land, and that no occupation is lowlier than farming. Seeing a field that had been plowed across its width, he said to the field that even if it were plowed lengthwise as well, doing business was better than farming it.
08.why: The Gemara is stringing together sayings of Rabbi Elazar; this one leads into more sayings comparing trade with farming, from Rav, Rava and Rav Pappa.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who speaks to a plowed field about how little farming pays.

08.flag: Mostly sayings; the only event is Rabbi Elazar's one remark to a field.

09.note: When Rav took leave of his teacher Rabbi Hiyya, Rabbi Hiyya blessed him that God should save him from something worse than death. Rav searched and found the verse "I find more bitter than death the woman." Indeed, Rav's wife tormented him: if he asked for lentils she made peas, and if he asked for peas she made lentils. When their son Hiyya grew up, he passed on his father's requests reversed, so Rav got what he wanted. Rav praised the trick, but told his son to stop, since it meant speaking lies.
09.why: The Gemara is collecting sayings and stories about wives, good and bad; this one is followed by Rabbi Hiyya's own troubled marriage and more teachings on a bad wife.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A student of Rabbi Hiyya whose wife did the opposite of whatever he asked.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Rav's uncle and teacher, who blessed him on parting.

people.name: Ḥiyya
people.about: Rav's son, who reversed his father's requests to his mother.

terms.meaning: A name for God.

10.note: Rabbi Hiyya's wife tormented him, yet whenever he found something she would like, he wrapped it in his shawl and brought it to her. Rav asked why, since she tormented him. Rabbi Hiyya answered that it is enough that wives raise our children and save us from sin. Separately, Rav Yehuda was teaching his son Rav Yitzhak the verse "I find more bitter than death the woman"; asked for an example, he said: your mother. The Gemara notes he had also named her as an example of finding peace with one's first wife, and explains that she was forceful but easily calmed.
10.why: The Gemara is gathering stories and sayings about wives, and goes on to define a bad wife and what a husband may do about one.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: A Sage whose wife tormented him, yet he brought her gifts.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's student, who asks him why he is kind to her.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage teaching his son, who names the boy's mother in two opposite verses.

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak
people.about: Rav Yehuda's son.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

10.flag: Combines two separate anecdotes (Rabbi Hiyya's wife; Rav Yehuda and his son) and begins mid-sentence across a page break.

11.note: Rabbi Yohanan reported a case of four sisters in Tzippori. The first circumcised her son and he died, the second circumcised hers and he died, and the third circumcised hers and he died. The fourth came before Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who told her: do not circumcise.
11.why: The Gemara is asking whether, for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, a pattern is set by two events or three. This case seems to show three, but the Gemara replies that the third sister may simply never have asked him, and that the case teaches that sisters together can set a pattern.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who told the fourth sister not to circumcise her son.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Reported the case, through Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba
people.about: Passed on Rabbi Yohanan's report.

terms.meaning: In Talmudic law, a pattern repeated enough times that it is assumed to continue; here, that a family's sons die from circumcision.

12.note: Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef came from the Land of Israel and reported a case brought before Rabbi Yohanan in the synagogue of Maon on a Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbat. One sister had circumcised her son and he died, and a second sister had circumcised hers and he died. When the third sister came before him, Rabbi Yohanan told her: go and circumcise.
12.why: The Gemara asks what the final ruling is: does a pattern of deaths start after two cases or three? This report is its answer, three. Abaye warns Rav Yitzhak to be sure of his report, since it permits something forbidden and dangerous.

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef
people.about: A Sage who brought this report from the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage who told the third sister to circumcise her son.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, the holiest fast day of the Jewish year.
The Sabbath. A circumcision done on the eighth day is performed even on Shabbat.

13.note: Relying on Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef's report, Abaye married Huma, daughter of Isi. Huma had been married to Rahava of Pumbedita, who died, and then to Rav Yitzhak son of Rabba bar bar Hana, who also died. Abaye married her, and he died too.
13.why: Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef had reported that a pattern is set only after three cases, so a woman widowed twice could remarry. Rava then criticizes Abaye: he himself had called that reporter unreliable, and a rule about circumcision need not apply to marriage.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who married a twice-widowed woman and died.

people.name: Ḥuma
people.about: Daughter of Isi; her first two husbands died, and then Abaye.

people.name: Raḥava of Pumbedita
people.about: Huma's first husband, who died.

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak, son of Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: Huma's second husband, who died.

14.note: A woman came before Rav Nahman wanting a divorce because her husband could not father children. He told her she was not commanded to have children. She asked whether a woman like her does not need a staff for her hand and a hoe for her burial, and Rav Nahman said that in such a case the husband is forced to divorce her. Separately, Rabbi Hiyya's wife Yehudit suffered terribly giving birth to twins. In disguise she asked him whether a woman is commanded to have children; he said no, and she drank a potion to make herself infertile. When he found out, he said he wished she had borne him one more set of twins, since their sons Yehuda and Hizkiyya and daughters Pazi and Tavi were twins.
14.why: The Gemara is asking whether a woman is commanded to have children, which decides whether she can demand a divorce from a husband who cannot father them. Both stories assume she is not, and the Gemara next tests that with a case that seems to show the opposite.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: A Sage who forced a husband to divorce his wife so she could have children to care for her.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: A Sage whose wife asked him, in disguise, whether women must have children.

people.name: Yehudit
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's wife, who drank an infertility potion after painful births.

people.name: Yehuda and Ḥizkiyya
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's twin sons.

people.name: Pazi and Tavi
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's twin daughters.

terms.meaning: The commandment to have children. The Sages here hold that it falls on men, not women.
The ketuba, which sets the money a wife receives if she is divorced or widowed.

14.flag: Combines two separate stories: the woman before Rav Nahman, and Rabbi Hiyya's wife Yehudit.

15.note: Rabbi Yitzhak reported a case of a woman who was half slave and half free, so she could marry neither a slave nor a free Jew. The court forced her master to set her free. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak explained that this was because men were treating her as ownerless, so she was falling into promiscuity.
15.why: The Gemara had said women are not commanded to have children. This case seems to show they are, since her master was forced to free her so she could marry; Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak answers that she was freed to stop the sexual misconduct.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak
people.about: Reported the case, through Rav Aha bar Rav Ketina.

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
people.about: Explains why the court forced the master to free her.

terms.meaning: A status that arises when a slave owned by two partners is freed by only one; such a person can lawfully marry neither a slave nor a free Jew.

16.note: A woman brought a fine wool robe into her marriage, listed in her marriage contract. When her husband died, his children took the robe and spread it over his body as a shroud, and she wanted it back. Rava ruled that the dead man had acquired it. Nanai son of Rav Yosef son of Rava objected to Rav Kahana that Rava himself had said the law follows Rav Yehuda, who lets a wife take back such items. Rav Kahana answered that even Rav Yehuda agrees the robe stays in the husband's possession until she collects it.
16.why: The discussion is about who owns property a wife brings into marriage at a fixed value: Rav Yehuda says she may take it back as a family heirloom. This case tests that view, and the Gemara links Rava's ruling to his rule that consecrating something frees it from a debt claim.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled the dead man had acquired the robe.

people.name: Nanai, son of Rav Yosef, son of Rava
people.about: Challenged Rava's ruling in a question to Rav Kahana.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Answered the challenge.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage whose ruling on a wife's property is debated.

terms.meaning: The ketuba, which lists what a wife brought into the marriage and what she receives if widowed or divorced.
Anything set aside for a corpse, like a shroud, may no longer be used for any benefit.

17.note: Rabbi Yohanan was sitting and teaching that leftover sacrificial meat burned at its proper time must be burned by day, but otherwise may be burned by day or night. Rabbi Elazar challenged him with a teaching that a late circumcision must also be done by day, drawn from the word "and" in the verse, and Rabbi Yohanan was silent. After Rabbi Elazar left, Rabbi Yohanan told Reish Lakish he had seen ben Pedat expounding like Moses from the mouth of God. Reish Lakish said it was not his own idea but a baraita in Torat Kohanim. Rabbi Yohanan went out and learned that whole work in three days, and understood it fully in three months.
17.why: The Gemara has explained that two early Sages disagree over whether the word "and" in a verse makes a late circumcision a daytime-only act. This episode shows Rabbi Yohanan holding the same view about leftover sacrificial meat, and being challenged on it.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: A great Sage who was silenced by his student's challenge and then mastered the source.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat, who challenged Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Rabbi Yohanan's colleague, who pointed out the source of the challenge.

people.name: Moses
people.about: Named in Rabbi Yohanan's praise of Rabbi Elazar's teaching.

terms.meaning: Meat of a sacrifice left past the time it may be eaten; it must be burned.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
An early collection of teachings on the book of Leviticus, also called the Sifra.
The Hebrew letter that means "and"; some Sages draw extra rules from it when it seems unneeded.

18.note: A man was climbing a palm tree when a thorn pierced his testicles, and a discharge like a thread of pus came out of him. Later he had children. Shmuel sent the case to Rav, who told him to go and find out where the man's children came from.
18.why: The discussion asks whether a man whose testicles were pierced counts as having crushed testicles, a condition that bars him from marrying into the community. The case seems to show such a man can father children, but Rav's reply suggests the children were not his.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who sent the case to Rav.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who doubted the children were the man's own.

terms.meaning: An injury the Torah lists as barring a man from marrying a Jewish woman by birth ("entering the congregation").

19.note: In Mata Mehasya a man's member had been cut like an open gutter; Mar bar Rav Ashi trimmed it into the shape of a quill and declared him fit. In Pumbedita a man's seminal duct became blocked and he emitted semen through the urinary duct. Rav Beivai bar Abaye wanted to declare him fit. Rav Pappi mocked him, saying that coming from a short-lived family he spoke short-lived words, since semen that does not pass through its proper place does not fertilize.
19.why: The discussion is about which injuries to the genitals bar a man from marrying into the community. Rav Pappa has just ruled that a cut shaped like a quill or a gutter is fit, and these cases apply that ruling and test where it stops.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: Reshaped an injured man's member and declared him fit.

people.name: Rav Beivai bar Abaye
people.about: Wanted to declare the Pumbedita man fit.

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: Mocked Rav Beivai's ruling and held the man unfit.

terms.meaning: Permitted to marry a Jewish woman by birth ("enter the congregation"), despite the injury.
Rav Pappi's insult: Rav Beivai's family was descended from the priest Eli, whose descendants were cursed to die young.

19.flag: The last segment (Shmuel's ruling on a punctured member, and Rava's discussion of it) is a legal ruling, not part of the two incidents.

20.note: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda came from the Land of Israel and reported that Rabbi Zakkai once recited a teaching before Rabbi Yohanan: an Ammonite woman is fit, her son by an Ammonite is unfit, her daughter by an Ammonite is fit, and if the father had not converted, the daughter is unfit. Rabbi Yohanan told him to go and teach it outside, and began explaining that its first parts were too obvious to need teaching. The rest of his answer comes after the story ends.
20.why: Rabbi Yohanan has just been cited as permitting the daughter of an Ammonite convert and a Jewish woman to marry a priest. This teaching says she is unfit, so he rejects it as unreliable.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: Brought this report from the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Heard the teaching and rejected it.

terms.meaning: A member of a neighboring nation. The Torah bars Ammonite men, even after converting, from marrying into Israel, but not Ammonite women.

terms.term: Go out and teach it outside
terms.meaning: A way of saying a teaching is unreliable and should not be studied in the study hall.

20.flag: Rabbi Yohanan's reply is cut off: his explanation of why he rejects the teaching continues after the story ends.
